# Abstract  {.unnumbered}

PURPOSE

More accurate risk prediction is needed for prostate cancer (PCa) to identify individuals at greatest risk of early-onset and clinically-significant disease. Current screening paradigms, such as prostate-specific antigen screening, pose risks due to over-diagnosis and over-treatment of indolent disease. Polygenic hazard scores (PHS) can predict age-at-diagnosis of PCa and are being tested in prospective clinical screening trials. We evaluated the performance of the latest PHS model for PCa (PHS601) in two Norwegian populations.

MATERIALS AND METHODS

We assessed PHS601 performance in two Norwegian cohorts (N = `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` and N = `{r} format(p212_sample_size[[1, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`) for predicting age-at-diagnosis of PCa and aggressive PCa. In a subset with whole-genome sequencing (N = `{r} format(wgs_summary[[1, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`), we compared PHS601 performance to screening for rare pathogenic variants, including HOXB13. 

RESULTS

PHS601 effectively stratified participants by risk in both cohorts (HR per SD = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2))` [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`] and `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2))` [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`]). Among individuals with whole-genome sequencing, the top 1.7\% of PHS values conferred `{r} round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 1)`-fold higher risk than the median (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2))` [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]), exceeding the risk associated with HOXB13 pathogenic variants (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "estimate"], 2))` [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`]; 1.7\% carrier frequency). 

CONCLUSION

These findings support the potential utility of PHS601 in a precision screening paradigm for PCa.

# Introduction

Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer among men worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality [@bray2024]. Although early detection can reduce deaths from PCa, population screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is limited by false positives, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment, particularly of indolent disease [@ilic2013; @roobol2025]. Therefore, there is a clinical need to identify men at elevated risk of clinically significant or metastatic PCa to focus early screening and downstream diagnostics (e.g., MRI), while minimizing harms.

PCa is highly heritable (~42%) [@lichtenstein2000] with risk influenced by rare pathogenic variants (RPVs) as well as common variants. RPVs, such as in BRCA1, BRCA2, and HOXB13, confer large increases in risk, but occur at low frequencies in the general population [@seibert2023]. Polygenic models combine many common variants with small effects to estimate inherited risk. Furthermore, polygenic hazard scores (PHS) use time-to-event modeling, which allows for prediction of age at diagnosis [@desikan2017; @seibert2018; @huynh-le2021]. The latest age-of-onset model for PCa, PHS601 [@vassy2024], is being implemented in a clinical trial of precision prostate cancer screening in the United States Department of Veterans Affairs healthcare system (Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05926102).

Recent PCa PHS models were developed in large, multi-ethnic cohorts and show robust stratification, but external validation in Nordic populations is limited. Here, we performed external validation of PHS601 in two Norwegian cohorts: a population study (Hordaland Health Studies; HUSK) and a clinical cohort enriched for family history of cancer (Norwegian Familial Cancer Study; NFCS). We evaluated whether PHS601 stratifies risk of PCa and aggressive PCa. We also leveraged whole-genome sequencing to compare PHS-based risk stratification with RPV carrier status, including HOXB13. Our aim was to establish the performance of PHS601 for age-specific risk prediction in Norwegian men as a step toward local implementation in a prospective clinical trial of genomically-informed cancer screening. 

# Methods

## Study Population

Two Norwegian cohorts were included in this study. The first cohort was the Hordaland Health Studies (Helseundersøkelsene i Hordaland; HUSK) with 35,515 participants. This cohort was recruited from Rogaland county in western Norway in two waves. The first wave was in 1992-1993 and the second wave was in 1997-1999. Analyses were restricted to the `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[2, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` male participants in HUSK. The second cohort was the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS) with 15,769 participants [@mattingsdal2021]. Participants in this cohort were recruited in 1980-1995 from all of Norway via self-report based on over-representation of cancer in their families. Analyses were restricted to the `{r} format(p212_sample_size[[2, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` male participants in NFCS.

## Characterization of PCa Cases

In both cohorts, PCa cases were defined as participants with ICD10 code C61. Diagnosis date was the first instance of this ICD10 code in the Cancer Registry of Norway, which has been found to be 98.8% complete [@larsen2009]. Controls were limited to males and censored at age of last observation. We did not remove individuals with other cancer diagnoses, who were therefore included in controls. Aggressive disease was defined according to metastasis codes `{r} metastase_strict[1:length(metastase_strict)-1]`, and `{r} metastase_strict[length(metastase_strict)]` in the Norwegian Cancer Registry, corresponding to disease that extends to lymph nodes inside or outside the same body region, organ metastasis outside the body region, and microscopic or macroscopic ingrowth into neighboring structures. 

## Genotyping and PHS calculation

### Genotyping

HUSK participants were genotyped at deCODE Genetics (https://www.decode.com/) in two batches (10,083 and 25,432 individuals in batch 1 and 2, respectively) using a customized Illumina GSA v3 array (687,316 genotyped variants). Prior to phasing and imputation, genotyping data were QCed separately for each batch using plink2 [@purcell2007]. QC steps for variants included removal of indels, non-ATGC, strand-ambiguous, poorly-genotyped (plink2's option: --geno 0.05), non-autosomal and rare (--maf 0.05) variants as well as variants with extreme deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (--hwe 1E-50 midp keep-fewhet). Chromosomal strand and allele order for the remaining variants were aligned based on the HGDP + 1KG reference panel from gnomAD [@koenig2024], and variants with alleles that were not possible to align to the reference as well as variants with MAF deviating from the reference by more than 30% were removed. Resulting genotypes from two batches were merged. Variants with high missingness (--geno 0.02) and individuals with poor genotyping rate (--mind 0.05) were removed from the merged data. The combined dataset was then phased and imputed with Beagle 5.4 (version 27May24.118) using the HGDP + 1KG reference panel. The resulting dataset contained 35,476 participants and 76,413,521 autosomal variants.

For the NFCS cohort, genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD, USA), following the manufacturer’s protocol, and analyzed using the Illumina OmniExpress 24 v1.1 chip at deCODE genetics (Reykjavik, Iceland). The genotyped dataset consisted of 713,014 SNPs. Genotype data were imputed using the HRC v1.1 reference panel following the same imputation protocol as The Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort [@corfield2024]. After imputation, the dataset consisted of 39,111,193 autosomal variants.

### Harmonization of alleles and calculation of PHS

The list of variants used by the PHS601 model, and their effect sizes, were acquired by contacting the authors [@vassy2024]. Chromosome X imputation was not available in our genotype data so the 21 SNPs in the original model on chromosome X were removed leaving 580 SNPs. Imputed genotype data in each cohort and model variants were matched by genomic position and alleles, resulting in 519 variants (in HUSK) and 557 variants (in NFCS) used for PHS computation. Strand-ambiguous variants were retained, after verifying that no strand flips were present among non-strand ambiguous SNPs in either of the two cohorts. Polygenic hazard scores were calculated for each cohort using `plink --score` [@purcell2007].

## Whole-genome sequencing

### Sequencing

The whole-genome sequencing data were generated at deCODE Genetics on samples from 2,576 participants from the NFCS cohort as described in @ivarsdottir2024. The samples were sequenced using Illumina HiSeqX and NovaSeq sequencing platforms with a total of 8,034 lanes, and all samples were prepared without PCR. Duplicated samples were discarded based on sequencing yield and only samples with a genome-wide average coverage of 20× and higher were included. `read_haps` was used to detect and remove contaminated samples [@eggertsson2021]. The average genome-wide sequencing coverage was 37.2X (SD = 6.3; minimum = 20.1X; maximum = 98.5X) and joint variant calling was performed using GraphTyper (v.2.7.5) [@eggertsson2017].

### Variant calling and classification of RPVs

Identification of RPVs in the WGS dataset was performed using the Cancer Predisposition Sequencing Reporter – CPSR v2.2.0 [@nakken2021]. Specifically, we used CPSR to screen WGS variant calls for heterozygous and homozygous SNVs/InDels in high-penetrance prostate cancer genes, including BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, PALB2, CHEK2, HOXB13, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, TP53, and EPCAM. Coding variants in these genes classified as pathogenic according to ClinVar (release 2025_03) were considered RPVs. Of note, the HOXB13 G84E variant (rs138213197) was included in PHS601 and was also identified among the RPVs in whole-genome sequenced participants. All participants carrying the G84E mutation in WGS data also carried rs138213197 in the imputed genotype data.

## Statistical Analysis

### Polygenic hazard score performance evaluation

Polygenic hazard scores were evaluated in both cohorts using Cox proportional hazards models using the `coxph` function from the `survival` package in `R` [@survival-package]. Polygenic hazard scores were centered and scaled prior to model fit. Performance of each model is reported as HR, which represents the increase in risk for a one-SD increase in PHS, with 95% confidence intervals (CI), p-values, and Harrell's concordance index (C-index). In addition, we used the metrics of HR~80/20~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the bottom 20% of PHS, and HR~80/50~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the median PHS. For these metrics, 95% confidence intervals were generated using `{r} bootstrap_iters` bootstrap iterations. For plotting of incidence curves, participants were separated by centile ranges of PHS into three groups: 0-20%, 20-80%, and 80-100%. All Cox models were evaluated for the proportional hazards assumption using `cox.zph` and by inspecting plots of the Schoenfeld residuals versus time [@grambsch1994]. For models that did not meet these assumptions, we performed sensitivity analysis with time-dependent covariates and a linear time transform (i.e., PHS $\cdot$ age) for the time-dependent PHS with the `tt` function. 

### HOXB13 variant effects and comparison to polygenic risk

We assessed the effect of RPVs on risk prediction using WGS data from the whole-genome sequenced subset of the NFCS cohort. First, we tested whether RPVs in any of the twelve genes were at higher frequency among cases than controls using the one-sided Fisher's exact test. We tested this for each of the twelve RPV-containing genes and for an additional variable indicating if participants carried an RPV in any of the twelve genes for a total of thirteen tests. The p-values from the Fisher's tests were adjusted using the Benjamini & Hochberg correction. Among these tests, we found only one gene in which RPVs were at elevated frequency among the cases than the controls, which was HOXB13. This gene was then used in a Cox survival analysis to estimate the risk of PCa associated with carrying this pathogenic variant. This model was evaluated based on the HR between carriers and non-carriers as well as the C-index. To compare the HOXB13 carriers to PHS, we subgrouped the dataset for individuals with both WGS and genotyping, refit the Cox model of PHS with this smaller sample, and calculated the HR for a similar proportion of individuals as were HOXB13 carriers. In this case, 1.7% of participants carried a HOXB13 mutation so we calculated the HR between the top 1.7% of PHS and the remaining 98.3% of subjects. 

### Comparison with Norwegian Cancer Registry data

To evaluate how generalizable our results were to the population of Norway, we compared the cumulative incidence in each cohort for both PCa (any stage) and for aggressive PCa to the cumulative incidence from the Cancer Registry of Norway (using the same ICD10 code and metastasis codes as before). We used cancer registry data for PCa cases in Norway for the years 2014-2017 as reported by @huynh-le2020a as annualized age-specific incidence rate binned by 5-year age groups. To convert the 5-year incidence rate into cumulative incidence, we fit a log-linear model to the average incidence for each 5-year age group. For PCa, the best fit was a log-quadratic model and for aggressive PCa the best fit was a log-linear model. We then predicted the annualized incidence from this model and calculated the cumulative incidence from the cumulative sum of cases. We compared these to the cumulative incidence derived from the Cox proportional hazards model for each phenotype (PCa or aggressive PCa) in each cohort. We then stratified the cumulative incidence curves by the HRs corresponding to the top 20% and bottom 20% of PHS from the Cox proportional hazards model fit to the HUSK data.

# Results

## PHS601 stratified PCa risk in two Norwegian cohorts

Participants with higher genetic risk scores in PHS601 showed greater risk of early diagnosis in both Norwegian cohorts. In the HUSK cohort (`{r} p2521_sample_size[1, 3]` cases and  `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS was associated with an `r (round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[1, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-coxph}). Individuals in the top quintile of PHS had over `{r} floor(p2521[2, 3])` times the risk of those in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} round(p2521[4, 3], 1)` times the risk of the median individual (HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}A). Results were similar in the NFCS cohort (`{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` cases and `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 4]` controls), where each SD increase in PHS conferred a twofold greater risk (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[1, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-coxph}), with HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[2, 3], 2))` (95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[2, 5], 2))`\]) and HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[4, 3], 2))` (95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}B).

In both cohorts, proportional hazards tests and plots of weighted residuals revealed a negative trend in hazard ratios with age (HUSK: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p2521_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[1, "p"])`; NFCS: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p212_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[1, "p"])`; @{supptab-zph}; @{suppfig-zph}) indicating that the effect of PHS diminished with age. To model this, we fit an extended Cox model with a linear time-dependent PHS term (intercept at age 40). At age 40, each SD increase in PHS was associated with a `{r} sprintf("%.1f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 1))`-fold (HUSK: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[3, "p.value"]])`; @{supptab-tt}) and `{r} sprintf("%.1f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 0))`-fold (NFCS: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) higher risk, declining by approximately `r round(1 - p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% and `r round(1 - p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% per year, respectively (HUSK: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 3))`, `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 3))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[4, "p.value"]])`; NFCS: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 3))`, `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 3))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[4, "p.value"]])`). However, the time-varying effects were weak and residual plots showed high variability, so we present the simpler proportional hazards models in the main results and figures.

## PHS601 was associated with aggressive PCa in Norwegian cohorts

In addition to evaluating the performance of PHS601 in stratifying individuals based on risk of PCa at any stage, we were also interested in the association of PHS601 with aggressive disease. In the HUSK cohort (`{r} p2521_sample_size[2, 3]` aggressive cases and `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[2, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS was associated with a `{r} (round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of aggressive disease (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[2, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-coxph}). Individuals in the top quintile of PHS had `{r} floor(p2521_meta[2, 3])`-fold the risk of those in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[2, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and twice the risk of the median individual (HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[4, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}A). Similarily, in the NFCS cohort (`{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` aggressive cases and `{r} format(p212_sample_size[[2, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS conferred a `{r} (round(p212_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of aggressive disease (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[2, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-coxph}), with HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[2, 3], 2))` (95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[4, 3], 2))` (95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}B). Proportional hazards assumptions were not violated in either cohort based on statistical tests and weighted residual plots (HUSK: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p2521_zph[2, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[2, "p"])`; NFCS: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p212_zph[2, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[2, "p"])`; @{supptab-zph}; @{suppfig-zph}).

## WGS did not reveal any population-specific effect of HOXB13 on PCa risk in the NFCS cohort

We compared RPVs and PHS in predicting PCa risk in the NFCS cohort (as the HUSK cohort did not include WGS data). Analyses were restricted to `{r} wgs_summary$wgs_1` participants with both WGS and genotyping (`{r} wgs_summary$status_1` cases and `{r} wgs_summary$wgs_1 - wgs_summary$status_1` controls) of whom `{r} wgs_summary$any_carrier_1` carried a predisposing mutation in one of the twelve target genes. Of the twelve potentially predisposing genes, only HOXB13 had an enrichment in the number of pathogenic variants among PCa cases compared to controls (OR = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[fisher$gene == "HOXB13_carrier", "estimate"], 2))`, 95% LCB = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[fisher$gene == "HOXB13_carrier", "conf.low"], 2))`, adj. p = `{r} pvalr(fisher[fisher$gene == "HOXB13_carrier", "p.adjust"], digits = 2)`; @{supptab-fisher}); the subsequent models focus on this gene. 

In independent Cox models, a one-SD increase in PHS predicted a `{r} (round(wgs_results[1, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% higher risk of PCa (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[1, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[1, "p.value"]])`; @{fig-hoxb13}; @{supptab-wgs}), while HOXB13 carriers had a `{r} round(wgs_results[2, "estimate"], 1)`-fold greater risk than non-carriers (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[2, "p.value"]])`). When both predictors were included, only PHS remained significant (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) whereas the HOXB13 effect was attenuated (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "estimate"], 2))`, p = `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[4, "p.value"]])`). The interaction term was not significant. Similarily, the PHS-only model had a C-index of `{r} round(wgs_cindex[[1, 1]], 3)` (SE = `{r} round(wgs_cindex[[1, 2]], 3)`) and adding HOXB13 to the model did not appear to improve discrimination (C-index: `{r} round(wgs_cindex[[3, 1]], 3)`, SE = `{r} round(wgs_cindex[[3, 2]], 3)`; @{supptab-wgs}). HOXB13 pathogenic variants occurred in `r round(wgs_summary$HOXB13_carrier_1 / wgs_summary$wgs_1 * 100, 1)`\% of participants. To enable direct comparison with this risk stratum, we evaluated individuals in the top 1.7\% of the PHS distribution against the median. This high-risk PHS stratum demonstrated `{r} round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 1)`-fold higher risk (HR~98.3/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]), exceeding the risk conferred by HOXB13 pathogenic variants. 

## Predicting population risk of prostate cancer onset based on HR from the HUSK cohort

We estimated risk stratification for PCa in the general population using HRs from our PHS models. For the population baseline incidence, we used log-linear models fit to data from Huynh-Le et al. (2020). We then stratified these incidence curves by the HRs corresponding to the top 20% and bottom 20% of PHS from the Cox proportional hazards model fit to the HUSK data. Analyses were conducted separately for any-stage PCa and aggressive PCa (@{fig-strat}).

Panel A of @{fig-strat} shows cumulative incidence of any-stage PCa by age and PHS stratum. For example, at age 75, an individual in the top 20% of PHS has an estimated cumulative risk of approximately 30%, compared with about 8% for someone in the bottom 20%. Relative to the population baseline, individuals in the top PHS quintile show substantially higher predicted incidence---roughly double the cumulative incidence by age 75. It is important to note that the apparent decline in incidence rate after age 70 in panel A is likely an artifact of reduced screening rather than a true decrease in disease occurrence (Huynh-Le et al., 2020).

# Discussion

PHS601 demonstrated substantial stratification of age at PCa diagnosis in two Norwegian cohorts. The HR per-SD increase in genetic risk, as well as HR~80/20~ and HR~80/50~, were comparable in magnitude to the performance of PHS601 in the original development and replication datasets [@vassy2024] and generally exceeded those of other polygenic hazard scores in Nordic populations, such as for Alzheimer's disease [@motazedi2022]. Robust stratification was observed in both the population-based HUSK cohort and the family history-enriched NFCS cohort. Despite the NFCS cohort being recruited based on self-reported family history of cancer and showing elevated cancer risk relative to the general Norwegian population (@{suppfig-comp}), PHS601 still effectively differentiated between lower and higher genetic risk individuals. These findings support the potential utility of PHS601 in a precision screening paradigm for PCa, both in the general population and among individuals with family history. 

For aggressive disease, we also found good stratification between high- and low-risk individuals based on PHS, and we see a similar magnitude effect in both NFCS and HUSK cohorts as in the original development set [@vassy2024]. This suggests PHS601 could be effective at identifying individuals at greater risk of aggressive disease and therefore with the greatest clinical benefit for further screening via PSA or imaging. Although PHS601 was not developed specifically for aggressive disease, it does appear to stratify for absolute risk of both aggressive and metastatic prostate cancer [@dornisch2025; @seibert2018; @seibert2023; @pagadala2023].

In addition to testing the performance of PHS, we also compared PHS to screening for RPVs such as HOXB13. In general, the polygenic score appeared to be more informative than RPVs. A much larger percentage of the population is affected by a high risk score than is affected by currently known RPVs---high polygenic risk affects 50x more people than BRCA2 mutations [@seibert2023]---which means genetic risk scoring may be more useful at the population level. Lastly, our combined PHS and HOXB13 model did not reveal any additional population-specific effect of this high-effect-size variant.

Even though HOXB13 was not significant in the combined model of PHS and HOXB13, clinical interventions may differ between individuals whose phenotype arises from rare deleterious mutations versus those whose phenotype arises from the interaction of environment with the normal array of segregating genes of minor effect. For example, individuals with BRCA mutations may benefit from PARP inhibitors [@turk2018]. Furthermore, RPVs and PHSes have different implications for genetic counseling, particularly regarding the risk to offspring in the case of RPVs. Therefore, there remains value in screening for these rare variants in appropriate clinical contexts.

We observed a time-dependency for PHS in the any-stage PCa model, though not for aggressive disease. While the time-varying effect of PHS was weak, we observed a significant negative trend in the HR of PHS with age in two independent cohorts such that the strongest effect of genetic risk was at the youngest ages (@suppfig-zph). This age-dependent attenuation of genetic risk is consistent with observations from other complex diseases and may reflect several biological processes. First, as individuals age, the cumulative burden of environmental exposures, somatic mutations, and stochastic cellular processes may increasingly dominate over germline genetic variation in determining disease risk [@jiang2021; @winkler2024]. Second, competing risks of death from other causes may differentially affect high-risk individuals, leading to a selected survivor population at older ages. Stronger genetic effects at younger ages have been well-documented for BRCA1/2 mutations in breast cancer [@kuchenbaecker2017] and across multiple complex diseases [@jiang2021]. The non-significant trend for aggressive disease may be explained by more complete case ascertainment for clinically-significant disease [@huynh-le2020a] or low power due to the small number of aggressive disease cases. These findings identify the age range where genetic risk stratification may be most actionable for prevention and early detection.

## Future Directions

While PHS captures inherited genetic risk, prostate cancer risk is also influenced by social determinants of health, lifestyle factors, and environmental exposures [@plym2023; @pagadala2024; @pagadala2024a]. Future work should investigate how these modifiable factors interact with genetic risk to refine risk prediction models, particularly in younger individuals with high genetic risk who stand to benefit most from early intervention.

The strong risk stratification observed in these population-based cohorts provides a foundation for prospective trials of risk-stratified screening in Norway. Before implementing population-wide genetic screening, cost-effectiveness analyses are needed to assess the economic value of PHS-based screening in the Norwegian healthcare context and identify optimal screening thresholds and age ranges.

One limitation of this study is that we did not have access to family history data or prostate-specific antigen measurements for all participants. While previous studies suggest family history adds limited information beyond PHS601 [@vassy2024], future work should explore optimal integration strategies for PHS with other clinical risk factors.

# Conclusions

We demonstrated that PHS601 performs well in independent, population-based cohorts from Norway, providing strong risk stratification not only for prostate cancer but also for absolute risk of aggressive disease. These findings support the development of prospective trials of risk-stratified screening in Norway. Given that high polygenic risk affects 50x more individiuals than known rare pathogenic variants, PHS-based screening has the potential for substantial population health impact. We recommend that future work focus on: (1) prospective clinical trials to demonstrate real-world effectiveness, (2) health economic evaluations to guide implementation, and (3) integration of genetic risk with modifiable lifestyle factors to maximize opportunities for risk reduction in high-risk individuals.

```{r tbl-coxph}
#| tbl-cap: HRs and C-Index for the any-PCa and aggressive-PCa models. HR is the increase in HR for a one-standard-deviation increase in PHS. HR~80/20~ is the HR between the top quintile and the bottom quintile of PHS. HR~80/50~ is the HR between the top quintile and the median PHS. 95% confidence intervals are model-based for HR and bootstrap-based for HR~80/20~, HR~80/50~, and C-index. "Any" = any stage of PCa, "Aggr" = aggressive PCa.

table_coxph = read_tsv("manuscript/figures_and_tables/table_coxph.tsv")

library(flextable)
library(officer)

# Create table
ft <- flextable(table_coxph) %>%
  fontsize(size = 6, part = "all") %>%
  border_outer(border = fp_border(width = 1)) %>%
  border_inner_h(border = fp_border(width = 0.5)) %>%
  border_inner_v(border = fp_border(width = 0.5)) %>%
  compose(
    j = "HR80/20",
    value = as_paragraph(
      "HR", as_sub("80/20")
    ),
    part = "header"
  ) %>%
  compose(
    j = "HR80/50",
    value = as_paragraph(
      "HR", as_sub("80/50")
    ),
    part = "header"
  ) %>%
  autofit()

ft
```



::: {#suppfig-zph}

![](manuscript/figures_and_tables/zph_tt.pdf){width=85%}

Assessment of the proportional hazards assumption for PHS using Schoenfeld residuals plotted against age. The solid blue line represents the estimated time-varying log hazard ratio from the extended Cox model with a linear time transform for PHS (95% confidence bands shown). The dashed blue line shows the log hazard ratio for PHS from the standard Cox proportional hazards model, and the dashed red line indicates a hazard ratio of 1.0 (log HR = 0). Divergence between the solid and dashed blue lines indicates violation of the proportional hazards assumption and time-dependency of the PHS effect. Panels **(A)** and **(B)** show results for any-stage PCa in the HUSK and NFCS cohorts, respectively; panels **(C)** and **(D)** show results for aggressive PCa in the same cohorts. 

:::

![](manuscript/figures_and_tables/cumulative_comparison.pdf){width=85%}

Comparison of cumulative incidence rates for PCa in two cohorts against national data from the Norwegian Cancer Registry. The red line represents the cumulative incidence observed in each cohort, while the black line depicts the overall cumulative incidence of PCa cases in Norway from 2014 to 2017, as reported by Huynh-Le et al. (2020). Panels **(A)** and **(B)** show incidence rates for any-stage PCa in the HUSK and NFCS cohorts, respectively; panels **(C)** and **(D)** show incidence rates for aggressive PCa in the same cohorts.
